'''Fresh Meadows''' is a [[neighborhood]] in the northeastern section of the [[New York City]] [[borough (New York City)|borough]] of [[Queens]]. Fresh Meadows was formerly part of the broader town of [[Flushing, Queens|Flushing]] and is bordered to the north by the [[Horace Harding Expressway]] and [[Auburndale, Queens|Auburndale]]; to the west by [[Pomonok, Queens|Pomonok]], [[St. John's University (New York City)|St. John's University]], [[Fresh Meadows, Queens#Hillcrest|Hillcrest]], and [[Fresh Meadows, Queens#Utopia|Utopia]]; to the east by [[Cunningham Park]] and the [[Clearview Expressway]]; and to the south by the [[Grand Central Parkway]].

Fresh Meadows is located in [[Queens Community Board 8|Queens Community District 8]] and its ZIP Codes are 11365 and 11366.<ref name="NYCPlanning"/> It is patrolled by the [[New York City Police Department]]'s 107th Precinct.<ref name="NYPD 107th Precinct"/> Politically, Fresh Meadows is represented by the [[New York City Council]]'s 23rd and 24th Districts.<ref>[http://www.nyc.gov/html/dc/downloads/pdf/queens.pdf Current City Council Districts for Queens County] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161222003335/http://www.nyc.gov/html/dc/downloads/pdf/queens.pdf |date=December 22, 2016 }}, [[New York City]]. Accessed May 5, 2017.</ref>

==History==
===Early history===
The name "Fresh Meadows" dates back to before the American Revolution. Fresh Meadows was part of the Town of Flushing, which had large areas of [[salt marsh|sal meadows]], such as the original "Flushing Meadows". The wetlands in the hilly ground south and east of the village of Flushing, however, were fed by freshwater springs, and thus were "fresh meadows". Fresh Meadows Road (which today follows the same route under a number of names, including Fresh Meadow Lane and part of Utopia Parkway) traversed the area, and served as the route from the landing place at Whitestone to the village of Jamaica. In ''[[New-York Evening Post|The Evening Post]]'' in 1805, farm owner James Smith advertised the sale of his 60-acre farm "on the road to Fresh Meadows and Flushing".<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/41500977/|title=For Sale, or to be exchanged for Property in the city of New-York|work=[[New-York Evening Post|The Evening Post]]|location=New York, NY|date=June 27, 1805|page=2|access-date=January 1, 2020|via=newspapers.com}}</ref>

During the [[American Revolution]], British troops marched through the area.<ref name= impressed/> [[General officer|General]] [[Benedict Arnold]] and his troops stayed at farms along the way.<ref name="ourstory">{{cite news|title=Long Island: Our Story / Our Towns / Queens|work=Newsday|date=February 22, 1998|page=H5|id={{ProQuest|279099066}}}}</ref> General Arnold drilled his troops in the area, on the current location of M.S. 216. In order to help move military supplies from British ships using the Whitestone Landing, a new road was built to connect the Fresh Meadows Road with [[Hempstead, New York|Hempstead]]. This road began at what is now the intersection of [[Utopia Parkway (Queens)|Utopia Parkway]] and 73rd Avenue, near a local landmark along the Fresh Meadows Road: the remnants of a large tree that had burned after being struck by lightning that was known as the "Black Stump". The road took its name from this feature, and was called "Black Stump Road".<ref>{{cite web|url=http://forgotten-ny.com/2006/03/fresh-meadows-queens/|title=Fresh Meadows, Queens|work=[[Forgotten NY]]|date=March 2006|access-date=September 24, 2014|author=Walsh, Kevin|archive-date=July 1, 2014|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140701100439/http://forgotten-ny.com/2006/03/fresh-meadows-queens/|url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.freshmeadows.com/story/History-of-Fresh-Meadows/162314|title=History of Fresh Meadows|work=Fresh Meadows website|access-date=September 24, 2014|archive-date=February 11, 2015|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150211070025/http://freshmeadows.com/story/History-of-Fresh-Meadows/162314|url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|last=Beyer|first=Gregory|title=An Outpost of the City, Within the City|work=[[The New York Times]]|issn=0362-4331|date=June 19, 2009|url-access=limited|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2009/06/21/realestate/21living.html|access-date=August 29, 2009|archive-date=February 23, 2012|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120223045358/http://www.nytimes.com/2009/06/21/realestate/21living.html|url-status=live}}</ref>

During the 19th century, a farming community known as Black Stump developed in the area. The Black Stump School was built before 1871.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://bklyn.newspapers.com/clip/41289719/|title=Long Island Items|work=Brooklyn Daily Eagle|date=February 15, 1871|page=3|access-date=December 29, 2019|via=Brooklyn Public Library; newspapers.com}}</ref> The school was expanded in 1900 and a second story was added in 1905.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/41289831/|title=Building Department Busy|work=Times Union|location=Brooklyn, NY|date=July 18, 1900|page=9|access-date=December 29, 2019|via=newspapers.com}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/41290229/|title=School Betterments in Queens Borough|work=Times Union|location=Brooklyn, NY|date=June 12, 1905|page=11|access-date=December 29, 2019|via=newspapers.com}}</ref> The remains of the Black Stump School were demolished in 1941 in order to build present-day Utopia Playground, located at 73rd Avenue and Utopia Parkway.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/41290364/|title=Work Started on Three New Play Centers|work=Brooklyn Citizen|date=September 20, 1941|page=2|access-date=December 29, 2019|via=newspapers.com}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|title=A Neighborhood Aspires to Its Name|last=Shaman|first=Diana|work=The New York Times|issn=0362-4331|date=December 21, 2003|page=11.7|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2003/12/21/realestate/if-you-re-thinking-of-living-in-utopia-queens-a-neighborhood-aspires-to-its-name.html|access-date=February 8, 2017|archive-date=March 25, 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160325044342/http://www.nytimes.com/2003/12/21/realestate/if-you-re-thinking-of-living-in-utopia-queens-a-neighborhood-aspires-to-its-name.html|url-status=live}}</ref>

For several years, the woods of Black Stump were rumored to be haunted because people heard strange sounds coming from the woods.<ref name="songs">{{cite news|title=Odd Tales of Many Cities: Ghost Songs Cease; Spook Goes to Jail|date=January 7, 1908|newspaper=The Washington Post|page=3|id={{ProQuest|144899254}}}}</ref> In 1908, the mysterious sounds were discovered to be coming from a recluse who lived in a small hut and sang [[Irish traditional music|Irish folk song]]s at night.<ref name=songs/>

=== Parsons Nurseries and Kissena Park ===
{{For|further details about the park itself|Kissena Park}}
In 1868, Samuel Parsons opened Parsons Nurseries, one of the earliest commercial gardens, near what is now Fresh Meadows Lane.<ref name="ourstory" /> With help of a team of collectors, Parsons Nurseries found exotic trees and shrubs to import into the United States, and its advertisements filled gardening magazines with depictions of these exotic plants.<ref name="higgins">{{cite news|last=Higgins|first=Adrian|date=August 31, 2017|title=Forgive this 1800s plant collector who brought us a mega-weed|newspaper=The Washington Post|page=11|id={{ProQuest|1985630417}}}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|last=Hanc|first=John|date=July 9, 2003|title=Open Secrets: The Hidden Pleasures of Our Parks: Kissena Park|work=Newsday|page=B3|id={{ProQuest|279692657}}}}</ref> During the late 1880s, Parsons Nurseries was importing 10,000 [[Japanese maple]]s into the United States each year with help from Swiss immigrant John R. Trumpy.<ref name="higgins" /> Parsons Nurseries also was the first to introduce the [[California privet]] in the United States from Japan.<ref>{{cite web|last=Wells|first=Nelson M.|title=Good Habits of Hardy Privets Prove Their Value in the City; Privet Grown As a Specimen|website=The New York Times|issn=0362-4331|date=November 12, 1939|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1939/11/12/archives/good-habits-of-hardy-privets-prove-their-value-in-the-city-privet.html|page=65|access-date=February 2, 2019|url-access=subscription|archive-date=February 3, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190203030828/https://www.nytimes.com/1939/11/12/archives/good-habits-of-hardy-privets-prove-their-value-in-the-city-privet.html|url-status=live}}</ref> Samuel Parsons' children, Samuel Bowne Parsons and Robert Bowne Parsons, later took over running the nursery. In 1886, Samuel Bowne Parsons helped renew the plantations of [[Central Park]] while serving as Superintendent of Parks.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://timesmachine.nytimes.com/timesmachine/1886/10/10/109787133.html|title=Renewing Central Park|work=The New York Times|issn=0362-4331|date=October 10, 1886|page=4|access-date=February 2, 2019|url-access=limited}}</ref>

Samuel Bowne Parsons gave the lake on his property the name "kissena", which he thought was the [[Chippewa language|Chippewa]] word for "it is cold".<ref name="oasis">{{cite news|last=Hanc|first=John|date=December 9, 2001|title=Kissena's Oasis|work=Newsday|page=H7|id={{ProQuest|279544089}}}}</ref> Kissena Lake was initially used as a [[mill pond]].<ref name="Beard19153">{{cite book|url=https://archive.org/details/americanboysbook00bear_121|title=The American boys' book of bugs, butterflies and beetles|author=Daniel Carter Beard|publisher=Lippincott|year=1915|pages=[https://archive.org/details/americanboysbook00bear_121/page/n298 289]–293|isbn=978-1-4400-9153-7 |access-date=July 9, 2018|author-link=Daniel Carter Beard}}</ref> Parsons later used the lake for [[ice cutting]], where surface ice from lakes and rivers is collected and stored in ice houses and use or sale as a cooling method before mechanical refrigeration was available.<ref name="oasis" /> The lake was also a habitat for [[wood duck]] through the 1900s.<ref name="Forest&Stream-1908">{{cite journal|date=March 28, 1908|title=Game Bag and Gun; Why Not Breed Our Own Wild Ducks.|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=Pbwo1phf26AC&pg=PA494|journal=[[Forest and Stream]]|volume=70|issue=13|page=494|access-date=July 9, 2018}}</ref> Just east of the lake was a water pumping station.<ref name="ElectricityWilcox19162">{{cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=SbMvAQAAMAAJ&pg=PA7|title=Report of Delos F. Wilcox, deputy commissioner: to the Commissioner of Water Supply, Gas and Electricity : in relation to the Citizens Water Supply Company of Newtown: October 7, 1916|author1=New York (N.Y.). Dept. of Water Supply, Gas and Electricity|author2=Delos Franklin Wilcox|author3=Citizens Water Supply Co. of Newtown|year=1916|pages=171–174, 219–220, 323|access-date=July 9, 2018}}</ref>

By 1898, Samuel Bowne Parsons' son, George H. Parsons, had taken over as superintendent of Parsons Nurseries.<ref name="obit">{{cite news|url=https://timesmachine.nytimes.com/timesmachine/1898/04/15/102490448.pdf|title=Obituary Notes|work=The New York Times|issn=0362-4331|date=April 15, 1898|page=7|access-date=February 2, 2019|url-access=limited|archive-date=December 16, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211216052649/https://timesmachine.nytimes.com/timesmachine/1898/04/15/102490448.pdf|url-status=live}}</ref> Later that year, George was found in the lavatory by his father; he had died of heart failure.<ref name="obit" /> Parsons Nurseries closed in 1901,<ref>{{cite web|title=Flushing's Claim to Floral Fame; French Huguenots Made It the Garden Spot of America in the Eighteenth Century.|website=The New York Times|issn=0362-4331|date=January 10, 1926|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1926/01/10/archives/flushings-claim-to-floral-fame-french-huguenots-made-it-the-garden.html|page=E21|access-date=February 2, 2019|url-access=subscription|archive-date=February 3, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190203084944/https://www.nytimes.com/1926/01/10/archives/flushings-claim-to-floral-fame-french-huguenots-made-it-the-garden.html|url-status=live}}</ref> and Samuel Bowne Parsons died in 1906.<ref name="bustle">{{cite web|last=Shaman|first=Diana|title=If You're Thinking of Living In/Kissena Park, Queens; Near Flushing's Bustle, a Quiet Enclave|website=The New York Times|issn=0362-4331|date=March 5, 2000|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2000/03/05/realestate/if-you-re-thinking-living-kissena-park-queens-near-flushing-s-bustle-quiet.html|page=11.5|access-date=February 2, 2019|url-access=limited|archive-date=February 3, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190203030827/https://www.nytimes.com/2000/03/05/realestate/if-you-re-thinking-living-kissena-park-queens-near-flushing-s-bustle-quiet.html|url-status=live}}</ref> Two real estate developers, John W. Paris and Edward McDougal, bought most of the Parsons land, then built large houses as part of the "Kissena Park" residential development.<ref name="bustle" /> New York City bought the rest of the Parsons land and a few other land parcels to create [[Kissena Park]].<ref name="oasis" /><ref>{{cite web|title=In the Park Or Not|website=The New York Times|issn=0362-4331|date=April 28, 1989|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1989/04/28/arts/in-the-park-or-not.html|page=C34|access-date=February 2, 2019|url-access=limited|archive-date=February 3, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190203030525/https://www.nytimes.com/1989/04/28/arts/in-the-park-or-not.html|url-status=live}}</ref> A {{convert|14|acre|ha|adj=on}} tract of Parsons' exotic specimens was preserved in the modern-day park and is now the Historic Grove.<ref name="KissenaPk-WildSide-1988">{{cite web|url=https://www.nycgovparks.org/sub_about/parks_divisions/nrg/documents/NRG_Publication_Kissena_Park_The_Wild_Side_A_Guide_to_its_Natural_Areas.pdf|title=Kissena Park: The Wild Side; A Guide to its Natural Areas|last1=Feller|first1=Michael|date=December 1988|publisher=[[New York City Department of Parks and Recreation]], Natural Resources Group|access-date=June 2, 2018|archive-date=February 3, 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180203211700/https://www.nycgovparks.org/sub_about/parks_divisions/nrg/documents/NRG_Publication_Kissena_Park_The_Wild_Side_A_Guide_to_its_Natural_Areas.pdf|url-status=live}}</ref>{{rp|3}}

===Fresh Meadow Country Club===
In 1921, [[Park Slope, Brooklyn|Park Slope]] resident Benjamin C. Ribman and others from the Unity Club of Brooklyn were looking to build a golf course.<ref name= clubhouse/><ref name="impressed">{{cite news|last=Morales|first=Tina|date=February 25, 1990|title=Marshes, Meadows Impressed Explorers Neighborhood's heritage includes the last commercial family farm in the city|work=Newsday|id={{ProQuest|278200504}}}}</ref> The group chose the intersection of Fresh Meadow Lane and Nassau Boulevard as the site, because the land was suitable for golf and roads provided accessibility to other parts of the city.<ref name= impressed/> The 106 acres of land were purchased in late 1921, and another 26 acres were purchased the next year.<ref name="woodland">{{Cite news|url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/41310874/|title=Woodland Golf Club Purchases 18-Hole Course: New Links Organization Acquires Tract of 106 Acres in Jamaica|work=New-York Tribune|date=December 18, 1921|page=19|access-date=December 29, 2019|via=newspapers.com}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/41311155/|title=Fresh Meadow Golf Course Ready in June|work=The Evening World|location=New York, NY|page=25|access-date=December 29, 2019|via=newspapers.com}}</ref> [[A. W. Tillinghast]] designed the golf course.<ref name= woodland/>

Originally, the name was to be the Woodland.<ref name="newname">{{Cite news|url=https://bklyn.newspapers.com/clip/41310973/|title=Woodland Golfers Adopt New Name, Fresh Meadow|work=Brooklyn Daily Eagle|date=January 20, 1922|page=26|access-date=December 29, 2019|via=Brooklyn Public Library; newspapers.com}}</ref>  After the ''[[Brooklyn Daily Eagle]]'' realized that there was already a golf course name Woodland in Boston, the founders decided to name the course Fresh Meadow Country Club.<ref name= newname/> The name came from an area northeast of [[Flushing, Queens|Flushing]] even though the golf course was actually located southeast of Flushing, just south of what is presently the [[Long Island Expressway]] near 183rd Street.<ref name=fmcc/>

[[Fresh Meadow Country Club]] opened on May 30, 1922.<ref name="newcourses">{{cite web|title=New Courses Opened; Fresh Meadow and Fenimore Clubs Join Met. Golf Ranks.|website=The New York Times|issn=0362-4331|date=May 31, 1922|url-access=limited|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1922/05/31/archives/new-courses-opened-fresh-meadow-and-fenimore-clubs-join-met-golf.html|access-date=January 31, 2019|page=26|archive-date=January 31, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190131093309/https://www.nytimes.com/1922/05/31/archives/new-courses-opened-fresh-meadow-and-fenimore-clubs-join-met-golf.html|url-status=live}}</ref><ref name="twas">{{cite news|title=Fresh Meadows Up Close 'Twas an Early Modern Community|work=New York Daily News|date=April 8, 1999|page=9|id={{ProQuest|313652130}}}}</ref><ref name="fmcc">"[http://www.freshmeadow.org/intraclub/query/combo.html?category=about%20fmcc&branding=1&hitlistwidth=153 About FMCC: A Tale of Two Clubs]". ''Fresh Meadow Country Club''. Retrieved May 31, 2012.{{dead link|date=May 2016}}</ref> At the golf course's dedication, the first round of golf was played by former [[NCAA Division I Men's Golf Championships|NCAA golf champion]] [[Jess Sweetser|Jesse Sweetser]] and club professional Willie Anderson.<ref name= newcourses/> Sweetser won by two strokes.<ref name= newcourses/> People in attendance included [[New York State Supreme Court|New York State Supreme Court Justice]]s [[Mitchell May]], [[Edward Lazansky]], and Harry Lewis, and [[Borough president|Borough President]] [[Maurice E. Connolly]].<ref name= newcourses/>

The clubhouse opened on September 8, 1923.<ref name="clubhouse">{{cite news|url=https://bklyn.newspapers.com/clip/41315086/|title=New Fresh Meadow Club House Burns: Loss is $150,000|work=Brooklyn Daily Eagle|date=September 17, 1923|page=40|access-date=December 29, 2019|via=Brooklyn Public Library; newspapers.com}}</ref> Nine days later, the clubhouse burned to the ground from an explosion of a boiler.<ref name= clubhouse/> Firefighters from Flushing, Bayside, and Black Stump arrived but they were unable to save the clubhouse, in part because the nearest fire hydrant was a half-mile away, but they were able to stop the fire before it consumed an adjoining locker building and a two-story dormitory building.<ref name= clubhouse/><ref name="clubburned">{{cite news|url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/41315206/|title=$150,000 Club Burned 9 Days After Opening|work=New York Daily News|date=September 18, 1923|page=13|access-date=December 29, 2019|via=Brooklyn Public Library; newspapers.com}}</ref>

The [[PGA Championship]] was held at Fresh Meadow Country Club in [[1930 PGA Championship|1930]],<ref>{{cite news|last=Rice|first=Grantland|date=September 12, 1930|title=The Sportlight|work=The Baltimore Sun|page=19|id={{ProQuest|543442746}}}}</ref> and the [[U.S. Open (golf)|U.S. Open]]<!--was held at the course--> in [[1932 U.S. Open (golf)|1932]].<ref>{{cite news|title=Sarazen Wins National Open|work=The Baltimore Sun|date=June 26, 1932|page=S1|id={{ProQuest|543346930}}}}</ref> In 1937, the golf course hosted a charity game between [[John Montague (golfer)|John Montague]], [[Babe Ruth]], [[Babe Didrikson]], and Sylvania Annenberg,<ref>{{cite news |title=Ruth Serious About Match|agency=Associated Press|newspaper=The Baltimore Sun|date=November 12, 1937|page=18|id={{ProQuest|538086593}}}}</ref> a game that was watched by 10,000 fans, some of whom rushed the golf course and left Babe Ruth's shirt in tatters.<ref>{{cite news|title=Frenzied Crowd Stops Montague Exhibition|agency=Associated Press|newspaper=The Washington Post|date=November 15, 1937|page=18|id={{ProQuest|150906301}}}}</ref>

===Holliswood Homes===
Around 1939, Paul Roth bought {{convert|27|acre|0}} of land that had been part of the Klein farm and the Boggs farm.<ref name="acquire">{{cite web|title=Builders Acquire Jamaica Farms|website=The New York Times|issn=0362-4331|url-access=subscription|date=March 26, 1939|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1939/03/26/archives/builders-acquire-jamaica-farms-27acre-tract-in-park-area-will-be.html|access-date=February 10, 2019|page=157|archive-date=February 12, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190212012125/https://www.nytimes.com/1939/03/26/archives/builders-acquire-jamaica-farms-27acre-tract-in-park-area-will-be.html|url-status=live}}</ref><ref name= boggs>{{cite news|url=https://bklyn.newspapers.com/clip/41566287/|title=Old Boggs Home Being Developed|work=Brooklyn Daily Eagle|date=March 26, 1939|page=47|access-date=January 3, 2020|via=Brooklyn Public Library; newspapers.com}}</ref> The land was bounded by 73rd Avenue, 185th Street, Union Turnpike, and 188th Street.<ref name="204homes">{{Cite news|url=https://bklyn.newspapers.com/clip/41315377/|title=Paul Roth Project to Have 204 Homes|date=June 22, 1941|work=Brooklyn Daily Eagle|access-date=December 29, 2019|page=26|via=Brooklyn Public Library; newspapers.com}}</ref> The 204 homes were designed by architect Arthur E. Allen.<ref name= acquire/><ref name= 204homes/> Roth named the community Holliswood Homes.<ref name= boggs/> Houses were sold for an average of $7,400 each.<ref name= 204homes/> Roth had previously developed areas elsewhere in Queens, Brooklyn, and Long Island.<ref name= boggs/>

===Fresh Meadows housing and retail development===
In February 1946, the golf course's land was sold to [[New York Life Insurance Company]] for $1,075,000, {{inflation|USD|1,075,000|1946|r=-5|fmt=eq}}, in order to build a housing complex on the land.<ref>{{cite news|title=Famous New York Golf Course Victim of Housing Shortage|first=Gayle|last=Talbot|newspaper=The Washington Post|date=February 5, 1946|page=10}}</ref><ref name="141acre">{{cite news|title=N.Y. Life Acquires Large Housing Site: Buys 141-Acre Fresh Meadow Country Club in Flushing, Queens, for $1,075,000|website=The New York Times|issn=0362-4331|date=March 23, 1946|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1946/03/23/archives/ny-life-acquires-large-housing-site-buys-141acre-fresh-meadow.html|access-date=February 4, 2019|page=28|url-access=subscription|archive-date=February 4, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190204065945/https://www.nytimes.com/1946/03/23/archives/ny-life-acquires-large-housing-site-buys-141acre-fresh-meadow.html|url-status=live}}</ref> The Gross-Morton Company had also made an offer to buy the land, but it was not accepted.<ref name= 141acre/> The New York Life Insurance Company chose [[Ralph Thomas Walker]] as the chief designer, and it signed a contract with the [[George A. Fuller Company]], which had built the [[Flat Iron Building]], to construct the apartment buildings.<ref>{{cite web|title=Housing Contract is Let: Fuller Co. to Build Apartments on Fresh Meadows Site|website=The New York Times|issn=0362-4331|date=June 1, 1946|url-access=subscription|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1946/07/01/archives/housing-contract-is-let-fuller-co-to-build-apartments-on-fresh.html|access-date=January 30, 2019|page=45|archive-date=January 30, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190130110451/https://www.nytimes.com/1946/07/01/archives/housing-contract-is-let-fuller-co-to-build-apartments-on-fresh.html|url-status=live}}</ref> Construction cost the New York Life Insurance Company $35{{nbsp}}million (equivalent to ${{Inflation|US|35|1946|r=0}}{{nbsp}}million in {{Inflation/year|US}})).<ref name="unsettled">{{cite web|last=Tomasson|first=Robert E.|title=Ownership Change Unsettles Fresh Meadows|website=The New York Times|issn=0362-4331|date=May 20, 1973|url-access=subscription|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1973/05/20/archives/ownership-change-unsettles-fresh-meadows-fresh-meadows-unsettled-by.html|access-date=January 31, 2019|archive-date=January 31, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190131093249/https://www.nytimes.com/1973/05/20/archives/ownership-change-unsettles-fresh-meadows-fresh-meadows-unsettled-by.html|url-status=live}}</ref>

New York Life Insurance Company donated land on 69th Avenue at 195th Street to the city so it could build a school.<ref name="contracts">{{cite web|title=Contracts Approved for Queens School|website=The New York Times|date=April 12, 1947|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1947/04/12/archives/contracts-approved-for-queens-school.html|access-date=February 10, 2019|page=9|url-access=subscription|issn=0362-4331|archive-date=February 12, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190212012024/https://www.nytimes.com/1947/04/12/archives/contracts-approved-for-queens-school.html|url-status=live}}</ref> In 1947, the New York City Board of Education awarded contracts of over $1.8{{nbsp}}million (equivalent to ${{Inflation|US|1.8|1947|r=1}}{{nbsp}}million in {{Inflation/year|US}}) to construct P.S. 26, an elementary school with a capacity of 1,494 students.<ref name= contracts/> On April 21, 1947, ground was broken for the school's construction.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/41566154/|title=Start New School|work=New York Daily News|page=B44|access-date=January 3, 2020|via=newspapers.com}}</ref> The school, P.S. 26, also known as the Rufus King School, opened in February 1949.<ref name="formally">{{cite web|title=4 Queens Schools Formally Opened; Buildings Costing $7,500,000 Provide for Thousands of Elementary Pupils|website=The New York Times|date=October 11, 1949|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1949/10/11/archives/4-queens-schools-formally-opened-buildings-costing-7500000-provide.html|access-date=March 3, 2019|page=29|url-access=subscription|issn=0362-4331|archive-date=March 6, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190306043453/https://www.nytimes.com/1949/10/11/archives/4-queens-schools-formally-opened-buildings-costing-7500000-provide.html|url-status=live}}</ref> P.S. 173 opened soon afterwards, in September 1949, at 69th Avenue and Fresh Meadows Lane.<ref name= formally/> P.S. 173 was originally supposed to be built on the site of Utopia Playground one block west, but the school had been relocated due to opposition from [[Robert Moses]], the New York City parks commissioner.<ref>{{cite web|last=Marzlock|first=Ron|title=How Robert Moses Saved Utopia Playground|work=Queens Chronicle|date=November 21, 2012|url=http://www.qchron.com/qboro/i_have_often_walked/how-robert-moses-saved-utopia/article_27d78f36-a1bb-558a-84f1-43b5faa6ddb4.html|access-date=February 16, 2020|archive-date=February 16, 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200216181056/https://www.qchron.com/qboro/i_have_often_walked/how-robert-moses-saved-utopia/article_27d78f36-a1bb-558a-84f1-43b5faa6ddb4.html|url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{cite web | title=Utopia Playground Highlights: NYC Parks | website=New York City Department of Parks & Recreation | date=June 26, 1939 | url=https://www.nycgovparks.org/parks/utopia-playground/history | access-date=February 16, 2020 | archive-date=February 16, 2020 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200216181046/https://www.nycgovparks.org/parks/utopia-playground/history | url-status=live }}</ref>

The first twenty families moved into the Fresh Meadows Housing Development on September 2, 1947.<ref name= openqueens>"Open Queens Project". ''New York Amsterdam News''. September 6, 1947. p. 19.</ref> As a result of [[Housing segregation in the United States|housing segregation]], New York Life Insurance Company did not allow black individuals to live in the Fresh Meadows Housing Development.<ref>Brown, Earl (August 9, 1947). "Timely Topics: About Jim Crow Housing Projects". ''New York Amsterdam News''. p. 8.</ref> It was also built to house local [[World War II]] veterans.  The complex and its eponymous shopping center were among the first in the United States designed primarily to accommodate [[automobile]] traffic rather than pedestrian traffic.<ref name="goldberger">{{cite news|last=Goldberger|first=Paul|title=To Utopia by Bus and Subway|work=The New York Times|issn=0362-4331|date=April 17, 1981|url-access=limited|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1981/04/17/arts/to-utopia-by-bus-and-subway.html|access-date=August 29, 2009|archive-date=December 5, 2010|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20101205105441/http://www.nytimes.com/1981/04/17/arts/to-utopia-by-bus-and-subway.html|url-status=live}}</ref> Apartment rents were between $74 and $108 per month, which included gas and electricity.<ref name= openqueens/> In 1949, architectural critic [[Lewis Mumford]] described the Fresh Meadows housing complex as "perhaps the most positive and exhilarating example of large-scale community planning in this country".<ref>{{cite book|last=Kroessler|first=J.A.|title=New York Year by Year: A Chronology of the Great Metropolis|publisher=NYU Press|year=2002|isbn=978-0-8147-4750-6|url=https://archive.org/details/newyorkyearbyyea0000kroe|url-access=registration|access-date=January 31, 2019|page=[https://archive.org/details/newyorkyearbyyea0000kroe/page/254 254]}}</ref> The construction of the final residential building, a 20-story apartment building at 67th Avenue and 192nd Street, was completed and ready for occupancy in May 1962.<ref name="modelcommunity">{{cite news|last=Bartnett|first=Edmond J.|title=Model Community Marks 15th Year; Last Building Is Opened in 15-Year-Old Fresh Meadows Community|website=The New York Times|issn=0362-4331|date=May 13, 1962|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1962/05/13/archives/model-community-marks-15th-year-last-building-is-opened-in.html|access-date=February 4, 2019|page=R1|url-access=subscription|archive-date=February 4, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190204065936/https://www.nytimes.com/1962/05/13/archives/model-community-marks-15th-year-last-building-is-opened-in.html|url-status=live}}</ref> At the time the building's construction ended, 11,000 people were living in the Fresh Meadows Housing Development.<ref name= modelcommunity/>[[File:Lookingeast 2.JPG|left|thumb|Remnant of [[Long Island Motor Parkway]] {{circa|2008}} at [[Springfield Boulevard]] in nearby [[Oakland Gardens]] ]]

New York Life Insurance Company built a 12-acre shopping center on 188th Street at [[Horace Harding Expressway]].<ref name="newshopping">{{cite news |title=New Shopping Area for Apartment Residents: 12-Acre Site Being Developed as Store Center Adjoining Fresh Meadows Housing|newspaper=The New York Times|issn=0362-4331|date=February 13, 1949|page=R1<!--[https://timesmachine.nytimes.com/timesmachine/1949/02/13/issue.html (PDF p. 142)]-->|id={{ProQuest|105768551}}}}</ref> The shopping center was planned to include a [[Bloomingdale's]], a movie theater, Canterbury Shops clothing store, Mary Lewis, Ormond Hosiery Shop, [[F. W. Woolworth Company|Woolworth's]], Miles Shows, [[Buster Brown & Company|Buster Brown]] children's shoes, Selby women's shoes, [[Food Fair]], a [[Horn & Hardart]] [[automat]], Whelan's Drugs, [[Fanny Farmer]], Union News, Womrath's Book Shop, Barrett Nephews dry cleaners, and Harris Brothers delicatessen, a [[Bank of Manhattan]], a [[Jamaica Savings Bank]], and a [[United States Postal Service|post office]].<ref name= newshopping/> Bloomingdale's opened on May 24, 1949.<ref>{{cite web|title=Store Is Opening in Queens Tuesday; Bloomingdale's to Hold Preview for Invited List Tomorrow at Fresh Meadows|website=The New York Times|issn=0362-4331|date=May 22, 1949|url-access=subscription|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1949/05/22/archives/store-is-opening-in-queens-tuesday-bloomingdales-to-hold-preview.html|access-date=January 30, 2019|page=35|archive-date=January 30, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190130110520/https://www.nytimes.com/1949/05/22/archives/store-is-opening-in-queens-tuesday-bloomingdales-to-hold-preview.html|url-status=live}}</ref><ref name="kmart">{{cite web|last=Garbarine|first=Rachelle|title=Real Estate: Queens Shopping Center Draws K Mart for an Anchor|website=The New York Times|issn=0362-4331|date=October 9, 1991|url-access=limited|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1991/10/09/business/real-estate-queens-shopping-center-draws-k-mart-for-an-anchor.html|access-date=January 30, 2019|page=D21|archive-date=January 30, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190130110751/https://www.nytimes.com/1991/10/09/business/real-estate-queens-shopping-center-draws-k-mart-for-an-anchor.html|url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|title=Bloomingdale Store in Queens Open Today|website=The New York Times|issn=0362-4331|date=May 24, 1949|url-access=subscription|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1949/05/24/archives/bloomingdale-store-in-queens-open-today.html|access-date=January 30, 2019|page=32|archive-date=January 30, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190130110524/https://www.nytimes.com/1949/05/24/archives/bloomingdale-store-in-queens-open-today.html|url-status=live}}</ref> Century Meadows Theatre opened November 1949.<ref>{{cite web|title=No Coins In Slots at New Automat; Restaurant Planned for Fresh Meadows Site Will Have Trim Waitresses Serving|website=The New York Times|issn=0362-4331|date=December 18, 1949|url-access=subscription|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1949/12/18/archives/no-coins-in-slots-at-new-automat-restaurant-planned-for-fresh.html|access-date=January 30, 2019|page=41|archive-date=January 30, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190130110409/https://www.nytimes.com/1949/12/18/archives/no-coins-in-slots-at-new-automat-restaurant-planned-for-fresh.html|url-status=live}}</ref> In 1973, Bloomingdale's added a three-level extension to the store, on what had been a pedestrian plaza.<ref name= unsettled/> Five 36-year-old oak trees were uprooted to construct the extension, to the dismay of nearby residents.<ref name= unsettled/>

In 1972, [[Harry Helmsley|Harry B. Helmsley]] and the [[John D. and Catherine T. MacArthur Foundation]] partnered to buy the Fresh Meadows housing and retail complex for $53{{nbsp}}million from the New York Life Insurance Company.<ref name= twas/><ref name="sale">{{cite web|last=Oser|first=Alan S.|title=Metro Business; Fresh Meadows Sale|website=The New York Times|issn=0362-4331|date=October 8, 1997|url-access=limited|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1997/10/08/nyregion/metro-business-fresh-meadows-sale.html|access-date=January 31, 2019|page=B6|archive-date=January 30, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190130162150/https://www.nytimes.com/1997/10/08/nyregion/metro-business-fresh-meadows-sale.html|url-status=live}}</ref> The MacArthur Foundation acquired the property outright in 1995.<ref name= sale/> In 1997, [[Witkoff Group]] and [[Insignia Financial Group]] bought the residential property, and Federal Realty Investment Trust bought the commercial property for $215{{nbsp}}million.<ref name= sale/><ref name="NYDN-Sale-1997">{{cite news|url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/27848274/|title=Fresh Meadows sale; 215M for huge complex|last=Bertrand|first=Donald|date=October 10, 1997|work=New York Daily News|access-date=January 31, 2019|page=765|via=newspapers.com}}</ref>

Depot Buy Kmart Leases / Retailers to open stores in Fresh Meadows, Syosset|work=Newsday|page=A47|id={{ProQuest|279704185}}}}</ref> The Kohl's in Fresh Meadows was the first Kohl's location in New York City.<ref>Boswell, Brannon (June 2003). "Big-box comes to the Big Apple". ''National Real Estate Investor'' (Atlanta, Georgia). Volume 45. Issue 6. p. 16–17.</ref>

===Klein Farm===
[[File:195th St 73rd Av td (2018-10-30) 02 - Klein Farm.jpg|thumb|right|The former farmhouse of the Klein Farm on 73rd Avenue]]
Fresh Meadows was home to Klein Farm, the last surviving commercial [[farm]] in New York City, located on 73rd Avenue between 194th and 195th Streets.<ref name="down">{{cite web|last=Shepard|first=Richard F.|title=Down On the Farm in Queens|website=The New York Times|issn=0362-4331|date=September 26, 1971|url-access=subscription|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1971/09/26/archives/down-on-the-farm-in-queens-down-on-the-old-farm-in-faroff-queens.html|access-date=January 30, 2019|page=A1|archive-date=January 30, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190130110651/https://www.nytimes.com/1971/09/26/archives/down-on-the-farm-in-queens-down-on-the-old-farm-in-faroff-queens.html|url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|title=A Farm Grows in Fresh Meadows|work=Newsday|page=06|id={{ProQuest|278384876}}}}</ref><ref name="harvest">{{cite web|last=Hernandez|first=Raymond|title=Neighborhood Report: Fresh Meadows; A Harvest in Queens That's Out of the Past|website=The New York Times|issn=0362-4331|date=September 26, 1993|url-access=limited|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1993/09/26/nyregion/neighborhood-report-fresh-meadows-a-harvest-in-queens-that-s-out-of-the-past.html|access-date=January 30, 2019|page=A9|archive-date=January 30, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190130161900/https://www.nytimes.com/1993/09/26/nyregion/neighborhood-report-fresh-meadows-a-harvest-in-queens-that-s-out-of-the-past.html|url-status=live}}</ref> Adam Klein, from Brooklyn, bought the Voorhis farm in the 1890s.<ref name= impressed/><ref name= down/><ref name= appears/><ref name="belt">{{cite web|last=Kirby|first=David|title=Passing the Endurance Test; A 2-Acre Farm Belt At 194-15 73d Ave.|website=The New York Times|issn=0362-4331|date=May 30, 1999|url-access=limited|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1999/05/30/nyregion/passing-the-endurance-test-a-2-acre-farm-belt-at-194-15-73d-ave.html|access-date=January 30, 2019|page=11|archive-date=January 30, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190130110740/https://www.nytimes.com/1999/05/30/nyregion/passing-the-endurance-test-a-2-acre-farm-belt-at-194-15-73d-ave.html|url-status=live}}</ref> Klein bought the 200-acre plot of land for $18 per acre.<ref name="holdout">{{cite web|last=Hevesi|first=Dennis|title=A Farm, In Queens? For Now, Yes; A Last Holdout Is Sold, But Some Hope to Save It|website=The New York Times|issn=0362-4331|date=February 27, 2004|url-access=limited|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2004/02/27/nyregion/a-farm-in-queens-for-now-yes-a-last-holdout-is-sold-but-some-hope-to-save-it.html|access-date=January 30, 2019|page=B1|archive-date=January 30, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190130161836/https://www.nytimes.com/2004/02/27/nyregion/a-farm-in-queens-for-now-yes-a-last-holdout-is-sold-but-some-hope-to-save-it.html|url-status=live}}</ref> The family sold portions of the land over time, but kept the two acres surrounding the farm house.<ref name="down" /><ref name="appears">{{cite web|last=O'Grady|first=Jim|title=Neighborhood Report: Fresh Meadows; Down on the Farm: A City Spread Appears Headed for a Last Harvest|website=The New York Times|issn=0362-4331|date=July 29, 2001|url-access=limited|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2001/07/29/nyregion/neighborhood-report-fresh-meadows-down-farm-city-spread-appears-headed-for-last.html|access-date=January 30, 2019|page=CY4|archive-date=January 30, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190130110534/https://www.nytimes.com/2001/07/29/nyregion/neighborhood-report-fresh-meadows-down-farm-city-spread-appears-headed-for-last.html|url-status=live}}</ref> His son, Charles Klein, was born on the farm and operated it after his father's death in 1954 at age 89.<ref name="down" /> By the early 1990s, John Klein Sr. ran the farm as well as two larger farms, one in [[Riverhead, Long Island|Riverhead]] and one in [[upstate New York]].<ref name="harvest" /> The family had received many offers over the years to buy the land in Fresh Meadows. In 1991, the family declined an offer from the owner of a local pizza store, who wanted to buy the property in order to convert the family's home into a country-style restaurant.<ref name="harvest" /> John Klein Jr., the great-grandson of Adam Klein, was running the farm by the late 1990s.<ref name="belt" />

The farm gradually became unprofitable, and in 2001, John Klein Sr. signed a contract to sell the two-acre property to Flushing-based developer Audrey Realty, who wanted to build 22 two-family homes on the site.<ref name="appears" /><ref name="blow">{{cite news|last=Bertrand|first=Donald|date=March 6, 2002|title=Developer Dealt Blow: Councilman opposes Klein Farm plan|work=New York Daily News|page=1|id={{ProQuest|305732555}}}}</ref> The farm's last day open was November 21, 2001.<ref>{{cite news|last=Virasami|first=Bryan|date=November 21, 2001|title=Their Last Season On The Farm Fresh Meadows site to shut down today|work=Newsday|page=A8|id={{ProQuest|279482095}}}}</ref><ref name="root">{{cite news|title=Dissension Takes Root in Sale of Farm Stand|work=New York Daily News|date=March 1, 2002|page=8|id={{ProQuest|305691352}}}}</ref> Many in the community were opposed to the proposed sale, including the Fresh Meadows Tenants Association, the West Cunningham Park Civic Association, the Flushing Heights Civic Association, the Hillcrest Estates Civic Association, the Utopia Estates Civic Association, and the Utopia Park Civic Association.<ref name="root" /> The community later learned that the developer was owned by the family of Tommy Huang, whose permits to restore the landmark [[RKO Keith's Theater (Flushing, Queens)|RKO Keith's Theater]] in Flushing were revoked when he destroyed its lobby.<ref name="root" /><ref name="fit">{{cite news|last=Murphy|first=William|date=February 22, 2005|title=Not the right fit for them, Bayside residents fear developer with history of violations will be allowed to jam four homes on one lot|work=Newsday|page=A15|id={{ProQuest|279891377}}}}</ref> Huang had also admitted to failing to report a spill of 10,000 gallons of heating oil from an underground tank into the soil beneath the RKO Keith's Theater in 1999.<ref name="blow" /> John Klein Sr. completed the sale to Huang for $4.3 million in late 2003.<ref name="holdout" />

The land was located in a Special Planned Community Preservation District and required a special permit to build homes there.<ref name="appears" /> David Weprin, the neighborhood's representative in the [[New York City Council]], opposed granting the special permit.<ref name="root" /> Faced with strong community opposition, Huang and Audrey Realty decided not to go forward with the plan,<ref name="battleground">{{cite web|last=Kemp|first=Joe|title=Day-care center defies eviction by a notorious landlord|website=New York Daily News|date=August 2, 2009|url=https://www.nydailynews.com/new-york/queens/day-care-center-defies-eviction-notorious-landlord-article-1.394535|access-date=January 31, 2019|page=33|url-access=limited|archive-date=January 31, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190131093510/https://www.nydailynews.com/new-york/queens/day-care-center-defies-eviction-notorious-landlord-article-1.394535|url-status=live}}</ref> and they instead agreed to sell the land to a [[Westchester County, New York|Westchester]]-based developer, Steven Judelson.<ref name="hands">{{cite news|last=Bertrand|first=Donald|date=March 15, 2004|title=Farm Changes Hands Again: W'chester Developer Has Eye on Klein Property|work=New York Daily News|page=3|id={{ProQuest|305871480}}}}</ref> At the time, Judelson said he had not decided what to do with the land.<ref name="hands" /> The sale did not go through.<ref name="cutters" />

In 2005, Huang sent a proposal to the City Planning Commission to build 18 two-family homes on the site.<ref name="preserving">{{cite news|last=Bertrand|first=Donald|date=September 20, 2005|title=Pol, Neighbors Urge Preserving Old Farm|work=New York Daily News|page=3|id={{ProQuest|305982221}}}}</ref> The proposal was not approved, and a day-care center was opened instead.<ref>{{cite web|last=Beyer|first=Gregory|title=Living in Fresh Meadows, Queens: An Outpost of the City, Within the City|website=The New York Times|issn=0362-4331|date=June 21, 2009|url-access=limited|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2009/06/21/realestate/21living.html|access-date=January 30, 2019|archive-date=January 30, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190130110744/https://www.nytimes.com/2009/06/21/realestate/21living.html|url-status=live}}</ref><ref name="battleground" /> Huang attempted to evict the day-care center in 2009, saying that he needed to end the lease early in order to sell the property.<ref name="battleground" /> Huang settled with the day-care center to terminate its lease three months early so that Huang could sell the property to Fresh Meadows Jewish Development LLC for $5.6 million.<ref>{{cite web|last=Kemp|first=Joe|title=Klein Farm deal struck: Day care agrees to vacate, developers in negotiations|work=New York Daily News|date=September 11, 2009|url=https://www.nydailynews.com/new-york/queens/klein-farm-deal-struck-day-care-agrees-vacate-developers-negotiations-article-1.405304|access-date=January 31, 2019|page=77|url-access=limited|archive-date=January 31, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190131093508/https://www.nydailynews.com/new-york/queens/klein-farm-deal-struck-day-care-agrees-vacate-developers-negotiations-article-1.405304|url-status=live}}</ref> The sale did not go through.<ref name="cutters">Robinson, Alex (August 7, 2014). "[https://www.timesledger.com/stories/2014/32/audreyrealty_tl_2014_08_08_q.html Klein farm sold to tree cutters] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190130110244/https://www.timesledger.com/stories/2014/32/audreyrealty_tl_2014_08_08_q.html |date=January 30, 2019 }}". ''TimesLedger'' (Queens, New York).</ref> In 2012, Huang was convicted of [[embezzling]] over $3 million of federal funds that were intended to pay for children's lunches at Huang's Red Apple Child Development Centers.<ref name="cutters" />

Huang finally sold the property to Ziming Shen's Fresh Meadows Children's Farm LLC for $5.6 million in 2014.<ref name= cutters/> New York City fined Shen $1,600 after Shen's daycare center, Preschool of America, cut down trees and modified the driveway on the property without the required permits.<ref name= cutters/>

===Hillcrest===
{{maplink|frame=y|frame-align=right|zoom=12|type=shape|from=Neighbourhoods/New York City/Hillcrest.map|text=Map of Hillcrest}}
[[File:UnionTpke2.jpg|thumb|[[Union Turnpike (New York)|Union Turnpike]] in Hillcrest, 2007]]
Hillcrest is a neighborhood in the center of Queens; the name comes from its location on the hills between Flushing and Jamaica. Hillcrest stretches from the [[Grand Central Parkway]] to 73rd Avenue, between [[Utopia Parkway (Queens)|Utopia Parkway]] and [[Parsons Boulevard]]. Its main commercial street is [[Union Turnpike (New York)|Union Turnpike]]. Hillcrest is part of [[Queens Community Board 8]]. The [[ZIP Code]]s for the neighborhood are 11366 (Fresh Meadows and Flushing zip code) for anything above Union Turnpike, and 11432 or 11439 (Jamaica zip codes) for the southern part of the neighborhood (below Union Turnpike, north of Grand Central Parkway). It neighbors [[Kew Gardens Hills, Queens|Kew Gardens Hills]] and [[Pomonok, Queens|Pomonok]] to the west, Fresh Meadows to the north, Utopia to the east, and Jamaica Hills to the south. It is mostly made up of single-family homes, is in a relatively well-off public school district, and has a low crime rate.

As with many neighborhoods in the city, different residents have varying perceptions of its boundaries.<ref name="NYT 2023">{{cite web | last1=Buchanan | first1=Larry | last2=Katz | first2=Josh | last3=Taylor | first3=Rumsey | last4=Washington | first4=Eve | title=An Extremely Detailed Guide to an Extremely Detailed Map of New York City Neighborhoods | website=The New York Times | date=October 30, 2023 | url=https://www.nytimes.com/interactive/2023/10/29/upshot/new-york-neighborhood-guide.html | access-date=June 24, 2024}}</ref>

====History====
75th Avenue was originally known as Hell Fire Lane, then Quarrelsome Lane, and then Eiseman Avenue.<ref name= 75thAve>{{cite news|url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/41566518/|title=Want 75th Avenue Improved to Meet Convenience of Buses|date=April 13, 1929|work=The Chat|location=Brooklyn, NY|page=2|access-date=January 3, 2020|via= newspapers.com}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|url=https://bklyn.newspapers.com/clip/41566417/|title=Queens Clerk's Office: Crush of Business|work=Brooklyn Daily Eagle|date=January 9, 1906|page=22|access-date=January 3, 2020|via=Brooklyn Public Library; newspapers.com}}</ref>

In 1938 and 1939, Moss Brothers built approximately 550 homes along Utopia Parkway between Horace Harding Expressway and Grand Central Parkway.<ref>{{cite web|title=Jamaica Home Site; Builders Plan 270 Dwellings on Utopia Parkway Tract|website=The New York Times|issn=0362-4331|url-access=subscription|date=November 20, 1938|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1938/11/20/archives/jamaica-home-site-builders-plan-270-dwellings-on-utopia-parkway.html|access-date=February 10, 2019|page=187|archive-date=February 12, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190212011959/https://www.nytimes.com/1938/11/20/archives/jamaica-home-site-builders-plan-270-dwellings-on-utopia-parkway.html|url-status=live}}</ref><ref name="19homes">{{cite web|title=19 Jamaica Homes Sold; Builders Report Rising Demand in Hillcrest Community|website=The New York Times|date=June 11, 1939|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1939/06/11/archives/19-jamaica-homes-sold-builders-report-rising-demand-in-hillcrest.html|access-date=February 10, 2019|page=RE9|archive-date=February 12, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190212012020/https://www.nytimes.com/1939/06/11/archives/19-jamaica-homes-sold-builders-report-rising-demand-in-hillcrest.html|url-status=live}}</ref> Moss Brothers hired architect Arthur E. Allen to design the homes.<ref name= 19homes/><ref name="active">{{cite web|title=Builders Active on Long Island; Sales and Home Construction Establishing High Record for Summer Season|website=The New York Times|date=July 16, 1939|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1939/07/16/archives/builders-active-on-long-island-sales-and-home-construction.html|access-date=February 10, 2019|page=129|archive-date=February 12, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190212011749/https://www.nytimes.com/1939/07/16/archives/builders-active-on-long-island-sales-and-home-construction.html|url-status=live}}</ref> The development was called Hillcrest Gardens.<ref name= 19homes/><ref name= active/>

===Utopia===
[[File:Bet-El Avi Dishi 2025 jeh.jpg|left|thumb|Bet-El Synagogue]]
Utopia is in the southeastern part of Fresh Meadows, bordered by [[Utopia Parkway (Queens)|Utopia Parkway]] to the west, 73rd Avenue to the north, 188th Street to the east, and [[Union Turnpike (New York)|Union Turnpike]] to the south.<ref name="NYTimes">{{cite web|last=Shaman|first=Diana|title=If You're Thinking of Living In/Utopia, Queens; A Neighborhood Aspires to Its Name|website=The New York Times|issn=0362-4331|date=December 21, 2003|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2003/12/21/realestate/if-you-re-thinking-of-living-in-utopia-queens-a-neighborhood-aspires-to-its-name.html|access-date=January 30, 2019|url-access=limited|archive-date=January 30, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190130110731/https://www.nytimes.com/2003/12/21/realestate/if-you-re-thinking-of-living-in-utopia-queens-a-neighborhood-aspires-to-its-name.html|url-status=live}}</ref> Utopia is part of [[Queens Community Board 8]]<ref name="NYCPlanning"/> and is often considered to be a part of Fresh Meadows, though ''The New York Times'' and the [[New York City Department of City Planning]] delineate Utopia as a separate neighborhood.<ref name="NYTimes"/> Utopia's residents includes many [[Conservative Judaism|Conservative]] and [[Orthodox Judaism|Orthodox Jews]], [[Israeli Americans]], [[Bukharan Jews|Bukharian Jews]], [[Chinese Americans]], [[Korean Americans]], and to a lesser extent, [[Russian Americans]], [[Indian Americans]], and [[Hispanic and Latino Americans]]. Utopia primarily consists of houses and tree-lined streets.<ref name="NYTimes"/>

The triangular-shaped Utopia Playground, at Utopia Parkway and 73rd Avenue, used to be the site of the Black Stump School, when the area was still called Black Stump.<ref name=NYTimes/> The school was later replaced by Black Stump Hook, Ladder, and Bucket Company, a volunteer firehouse.<ref name=NYTimes/> Today, it has a playground, a softball field, basketball courts, and [[American handball|handball]] courts.<ref name=NYTimes/>

It is bordered by the neighborhoods of Hillcrest to the west, Fresh Meadows to the north and east, and [[Jamaica Estates]] to the south. Utopia is also home to the Hillcrest Jewish Center and the [[Queens Public Library]] at Hillcrest, both located on Union Turnpike.

====History====
Simon Freeman, Samuel Resler, and Joseph Fried incorporated the Utopia Land Company in 1903.<ref>{{cite news|title=New York Incorporations|work=The New York Times|issn=0362-4331|url-access=limited|date=May 13, 1903|url=http://timesmachine.nytimes.com/timesmachine/1903/05/13/101997743.html?pageNumber=14|access-date=February 5, 2019|page=14}}</ref> The following year, the Utopia Land Company bought {{convert|161.25|acre|0}} of land between the communities of Jamaica and Flushing.<ref>{{cite web|title=In the Real Estate Field; Harlem Plots Bought for Improvement -- Ex-Gov. Morton's Purchase -- New Building at Broadway and Fifty-Fifth Street -- Dealings by Brokers and at Auction.|website=The New York Times|issn=0362-4331|url-access=limited|date=March 26, 1904|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1904/03/26/archives/in-the-real-estate-field-harlem-plots-bought-for-improvement-exgov.html|access-date=February 5, 2019|page=15|archive-date=February 7, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190207022150/https://www.nytimes.com/1904/03/26/archives/in-the-real-estate-field-harlem-plots-bought-for-improvement-exgov.html|url-status=live}}</ref><ref name="hebrew">{{cite web|title=A Hebrew Utopia|website=The New York Times|issn=0362-4331|url-access=limited|date=June 7, 1905|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1905/06/07/archives/sheffield-may-refuse-gas-commission-berth-would-rather-be-federal.html|access-date=February 5, 2019|page=16|archive-date=February 7, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190207022242/https://www.nytimes.com/1905/06/07/archives/sheffield-may-refuse-gas-commission-berth-would-rather-be-federal.html|url-status=live}}</ref> The Utopia Land Company intended to build a [[Cooperative|cooperative community]] for Jewish families interested in moving away from the [[Lower East Side]] of [[Manhattan]]. They intended to name the streets after those on the Lower East Side, where there was already a large Jewish population.<ref name= hebrew/>

After its initial acquisition, the company was unable to secure enough funding to further develop the area.<ref name="utopiainqueens">{{cite web|last=Schneider|first=Daniel B.|title=F.Y.I.: A Utopia in Queens|issn=0362-4331|url-access=limited|website=The New York Times|date=January 26, 1997|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1997/01/26/nyregion/fyi-313211.html|access-date=February 5, 2019|page=CY2|archive-date=February 7, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190207020604/https://www.nytimes.com/1997/01/26/nyregion/fyi-313211.html|url-status=live}}</ref> In 1909, {{convert|118|acre|0}} of the land was sold to Felix Isman of Philadelphia for $350,000, {{inflation|US|350,000|1909|r=-5|fmt=eq}}.<ref>{{cite web|title=Isman's $350,000 Purchase; Philadelphia Operator Buys Tract of 118 Acres Near Jamaica.|website=The New York Times|issn=0362-4331|url-access=limited|date=June 13, 1909|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1909/06/13/archives/ismans-350000-purchase-philadelphia-operator-buys-tract-of-118.html|access-date=February 5, 2019|page=14|archive-date=February 7, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190207020539/https://www.nytimes.com/1909/06/13/archives/ismans-350000-purchase-philadelphia-operator-buys-tract-of-118.html|url-status=live}}</ref>

The area remained farmland until 1935, when the land was bought by the Gross-Morton Park Corporation, run by George M. Gross, Alfred Gross, and Lawrence Morton.<ref name="plans">{{cite web|title=Plans for Buildings Filed by Architects: Variety of New Structures Are Projected in Manhattan, Bronx, Brooklyn and Queens.|website=The New York Times|issn=0362-4331|url-access=subscription|date=August 21, 1935|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1935/08/21/archives/plans-for-buildings-filed-by-architects-variety-of-new-structures.html|access-date=February 5, 2019|page=38|archive-date=February 7, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190207020659/https://www.nytimes.com/1935/08/21/archives/plans-for-buildings-filed-by-architects-variety-of-new-structures.html|url-status=live}}</ref><ref name="centres">{{cite news |title=Home-Building Centres|newspaper=The New York Times|issn=0362-4331|date=August 18, 1935|page=RE1<!--[https://timesmachine.nytimes.com/timesmachine/1935/08/18/issue.html PDF p. 86]-->|id={{ProQuest|101380138}}}}</ref> Gross-Morton had experience in building residential developments in Queens, such as when it had developed the land of the Belleclaire golf course in Bayside, around today's 48th Avenue and 211th Street.<ref name= plans/><ref name= centres/> In 1937, the company bought {{convert|27|acres}} of contiguous farmland on the south side of Black Stump Road (now 73rd Avenue) from the Klein family.<ref>{{cite web|title=Queens Farm Bought for Housing Project; 600 New Homes Planned for Jamaica-Hillcrest Site by Building Concern|website=The New York Times|date=February 12, 1937|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1937/02/12/archives/queens-farm-bought-for-housing-project-600-new-homes-planned-for.html|access-date=March 3, 2019|page=44|issn=0362-4331|url-access=subscription|archive-date=March 6, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190306050759/https://www.nytimes.com/1937/02/12/archives/queens-farm-bought-for-housing-project-600-new-homes-planned-for.html|url-status=live}}</ref> In 1939, it bought {{convert|117|acres}} of land that had been formerly part of the Klein Farm and the Wigmore estate.<ref name="54blocks">{{cite web|title=54 Blocks Bought for Home Centers: Gross-Morton Firm Announces Plans for 1,400 Houses on Queens Tracts|website=The New York Times|date=April 9, 1939|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1939/04/09/archives/54-blocks-bought-for-home-centers-grossmorton-firm-announces-plans.html|access-date=March 3, 2019|page=RE1|issn=0362-4331|url-access=subscription|archive-date=March 6, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190306050844/https://www.nytimes.com/1939/04/09/archives/54-blocks-bought-for-home-centers-grossmorton-firm-announces-plans.html|url-status=live}}</ref> The land included about one mile of land directly on Union Turnpike, on which it built about forty stores.<ref name= 54blocks/>

On the land it bought in Utopia, the Gross-Morton Park Corporation built [[American colonial architecture|colonial]] and [[Cape Cod (house)|Cape Cod-style]] homes with either two or three bedrooms, each on approximately {{convert|4000|sqft|0}} of land in the early 1940s.<ref name="NYTimes"/> Arthur Allen was the architect of the homes.<ref>{{cite web|title=Residence Planned at 16 Sutton Square; Mrs. Lili Havemeyer to Erect $30,000 Home There: Queens|website=The New York Times|issn=0362-4331|url-access=subscription|date=May 21, 1940|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1940/05/21/archives/residence-planned-at-16-sutton-square-mrs-lili-havemeyer-to-erect.html|access-date=February 5, 2019|page=47|archive-date=February 7, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190207020339/https://www.nytimes.com/1940/05/21/archives/residence-planned-at-16-sutton-square-mrs-lili-havemeyer-to-erect.html|url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.proquest.com/docview/105410572 |title=Building Plans Filed|work=The New York Times|issn=0362-4331|url-access=subscription|date=May 30, 1940|page=38|access-date=February 5, 2019 |id={{ProQuest|105410572}} }}<!--https://timesmachine.nytimes.com/timesmachine/1940/05/30/94834663.pdf--></ref>

In 1938, Paul Roth bought the portion of the Klein Farm on the north side of Union Turnpike, between 185th Street and 188th Street, to build 70 houses.<ref>{{cite web|title=70 Flushing Lots Added for Housing; Builder of Small Dwellings Buys Union Turnpike Tract Adjoining Development|website=The New York Times|date=November 18, 1938|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1938/11/18/archives/70-flushing-lots-added-for-housing-builder-of-small-dwellings-buys.html|access-date=March 3, 2019|page=41|issn=0362-4331|url-access=subscription|archive-date=March 6, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190306052440/https://www.nytimes.com/1938/11/18/archives/70-flushing-lots-added-for-housing-builder-of-small-dwellings-buys.html|url-status=live}}</ref>

The Batterman family owned and operated a farm on land bounded by Union Turnpike, Utopia Parkway, 75th Avenue, and 170th Street.<ref name="foch">{{cite web|title=Builders Acquire Farm in Jamaica: New Owners Plan to Erect 500 Homes on the Former Batterman Property|website=The New York Times|issn=0362-4331|url-access=subscription|date=June 12, 1938|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1938/06/12/archives/builders-acquire-farm-in-jamaica-new-owners-plan-to-erect-500-homes.html|access-date=February 10, 2019|page=182|archive-date=February 10, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190210152702/https://www.nytimes.com/1938/06/12/archives/builders-acquire-farm-in-jamaica-new-owners-plan-to-erect-500-homes.html|url-status=live}}</ref> In 1938, the Foch Building Corporation bought the Batterman Estate in order to develop it into a residential neighborhood, named University Manor.<ref name= foch/> The Foch Building Corporation had previously built 111 houses in what is now [[St. Albans, Queens]].<ref name= foch/>

==Police and crime==
Fresh Meadows is patrolled by the 107th Precinct of the [[New York City Police Department|NYPD]], located at 71-01 Parsons Boulevard.<ref name="NYPD 107th Precinct">{{Cite web|url=https://www1.nyc.gov/site/nypd/bureaus/patrol/precincts/107th-precinct.page|title=NYPD – 107th Precinct|website=www.nyc.gov|publisher=[[New York City Police Department]]|access-date=October 3, 2016|archive-date=July 2, 2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170702055554/http://www1.nyc.gov/site/nypd/bureaus/patrol/precincts/107th-precinct.page|url-status=live}}</ref>  The 107th Precinct ranked 11th safest out of 69 patrol areas for per-capita crime in 2010. The low crime rate was attributed primarily to the area's isolation and to local neighborhood patrols.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.dnainfo.com/new-york/crime-safety-report/queens/fresh-meadows/|title=Fresh Meadows – DNAinfo.com Crime and Safety Report|website=www.dnainfo.com|access-date=October 6, 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170415053352/https://www.dnainfo.com/new-york/crime-safety-report/queens/fresh-meadows|archive-date=April 15, 2017}}</ref> {{As of|2018}}, with a non-fatal assault rate of 22 per 100,000 people, Fresh Meadows's rate of [[violent crime]]s per capita is lower than that of the city as a whole. The incarceration rate of 191 per 100,000 people is lower than that of the city as a whole.<ref name="CHP2018" />{{Rp|8}}

The 107th Precinct has a lower crime rate than in the 1990s, with total major felony complaints decreasing by 83.5% between 1990 and 2025. In 2025, the precinct reported 3 murders, 24 rapes, 109 robberies, 259 felony assaults, 238 burglaries, 604 grand larcenies, and 356 grand larcenies auto.<ref>{{Cite web |title=CompStat 107th Precinct Report Covering the Week 9/14/2026 Through 9/20/2026 |url=https://www.nyc.gov/assets/nypd/downloads/pdf/crime_statistics/cs-en-us-107pct.pdf |access-date=23 September 2026 |website=CompStat}}</ref>

== Health ==
{{As of|2018}}, [[preterm birth]]s and births to teenage mothers are less common in Fresh Meadows than in other places citywide. In Fresh Meadows, there were 74 preterm births per 1,000 live births (compared to 87 per 1,000 citywide), and 6.7 births to teenage mothers per 1,000 live births (compared to 19.3 per 1,000 citywide).<ref name="CHP2018" />{{Rp|11}} Fresh Meadows has a relatively average population of residents who are [[Health insurance coverage in the United States|uninsured]]. In 2018, this population of uninsured residents was estimated to be 11%, which is slightly lower than the citywide rate of 12%.<ref name="CHP2018" />{{Rp|14}}

The concentration of [[particulates|fine particulate matter]], the deadliest type of [[air pollution|air pollutant]], in Fresh Meadows is {{convert|0.0078|mg/m3|oz/ft3}}, lower than the citywide and boroughwide averages.<ref name="CHP2018" />{{Rp|9}} Fourteen percent of Fresh Meadows residents are [[Smoking|smokers]], which is equal to the city average of 14% of residents being smokers.<ref name="CHP2018" />{{Rp|13}} In Fresh Meadows, 19% of residents are [[Obesity|obese]], 11% are [[Diabetes mellitus|diabetic]], and 29% have [[hypertension|high blood pressure]]—compared to the citywide averages of 20%, 14%, and 24% respectively.<ref name="CHP2018" />{{Rp|16}} In addition, 18% of children are obese, compared to the citywide average of 20%.<ref name="CHP2018" />{{Rp|12}}

Eighty-nine percent of residents eat some fruits and vegetables every day, which is higher than the city's average of 87%. In 2018, 79% of residents described their health as "good", "very good", or "excellent", about the same as the city's average of 78%.<ref name="CHP2018" />{{Rp|13}} For every supermarket in Fresh Meadows, there are 5 [[convenience store|bodegas]].<ref name="CHP2018" />{{Rp|10}}

The nearest large hospitals to Fresh Meadows are [[Queens Hospital Center]] in Hillcrest and [[NewYork–Presbyterian Queens]] in Flushing.<ref>{{cite web | last=Finkel | first=Beth | title=Guide To Queens Hospitals | website=Queens Tribune | date=February 27, 2014 | url=http://queenstribune.com/guide-to-queens-hospitals/ | access-date=March 7, 2019 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170204185507/http://queenstribune.com/guide-to-queens-hospitals/ | archive-date=February 4, 2017 }}</ref>

== Education ==
Fresh Meadows generally has a higher ratio of college-educated residents than the rest of the city {{as of|2018|lc=y}}. Half of residents (50%) have a college education or higher, while 14% have less than a high school education and 37% are high school graduates or have some college education. By contrast, 39% of Queens residents and 43% of city residents have a college education or higher.<ref name="CHP2018" />{{Rp|6}} The percentage of Fresh Meadows students excelling in math rose from 51 percent in 2000 to 71 percent in 2011, and reading achievement rose from 56% to 57% during the same time period.<ref name=":17">{{Cite web|url=http://furmancenter.org/files/sotc/QN_08_11.pdf|title=Fresh Meadows/Hillcrest – QN 08|date=2011|publisher=[[Furman Center for Real Estate and Urban Policy]]|access-date=October 5, 2016|archive-date=September 18, 2013|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130918064248/http://furmancenter.org/files/sotc/QN_08_11.pdf|url-status=live}}</ref>

Fresh Meadows's rate of elementary school student absenteeism is less than the rest of New York City. In Fresh Meadows, 15% of elementary school students missed twenty or more days per [[school year]], less than the citywide average of 20%.<ref name=":21" />{{Rp|24 (PDF p. 55)}}<ref name="CHP2018" />{{Rp|6}} Additionally, 86% of high school students in Fresh Meadows graduate on time, more than the citywide average of 75%.<ref name="CHP2018" />{{Rp|6}}

====Former====
In June 1873, the [[Central Railroad of Long Island]] opened a station, called Frankiston, on Black Stump Road, now called 73rd Avenue.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/41565961/|title=Long Island|work=The Brooklyn Union|date=June 14, 1873|page=2|via=newspapers.com}}</ref> It was east of the present-day [[Clearview Expressway]], where [[Cunningham Park]] is now. The railroad line continued northwest, along the parkland between today's Peck Avenue and Underhill Avenue, ultimately ending in downtown Flushing.

The origin of the name Frankiston is unknown. Loomis L. White, the railroad's second largest stockholder, had bought all the land surrounding the station in April 1871. The station's building was built by E.W. Karker & Co. of [[College Point, Queens|College Point]], April–May 1873.<ref name= seyfried>{{cite web|last=Seyfried|first=Vincent F|date=1963|title=The Long Island Rail Road: A Comprehensive History: Part Two: The Flushing, North Shore & Central Railroad|url=http://digitalarchives.queenslibrary.org/vital/access/services/Download/aql:336/SOURCE1?view=true|access-date=July 13, 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20151002160811/http://digitalarchives.queenslibrary.org/vital/access/services/Download/aql:336/SOURCE1?view=true|archive-date=October 2, 2015}}</ref>{{rp|147}} The train fare from Frankston to downtown Flushing was $0.30 ({{inflation|US|0.30|1873|fmt=eq}}).<ref name= seyfried/>{{rp|109}} The station was first included in railroad timetables in June 1873.<ref name= seyfried/>{{rp|147}}

On April 30, 1879, the station was closed and the railroad line was abandoned.<ref name= seyfried/>{{rp|147}}<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/41566033/|title=Long Island Railroad Abandoned|work=The New York Times|date=May 2, 1879|page=8|issn=0362-4331|access-date=January 3, 2020|url-access=limited|via=newspapers.com}}</ref>

====Proposed====
In the 1970s, an extension of the subway system along Horace Harding Expressway was proposed as part of the [[Program for Action]], but it was ultimately not built.<ref>{{Cite Routes Not Taken|page=253}}</ref>

===Highways===
The [[Long Island Expressway]] ([[Interstate 495 (New York)|I-495]]) connects Fresh Meadows with both midtown Manhattan and Long Island, while the [[Clearview Expressway]] ([[Interstate 295 (New York)|I-295]]) provides access to [[Bronx, New York|the Bronx]] and [[Interstate 95 (New York)|the New England Thruway]].

The [[Long Island Motor Parkway]], formerly a highway, is now used as a biking and walking trail, as part of the [[Brooklyn–Queens Greenway]].
